module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 985

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/985](https://www.erdosproblems.com/985)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos985

/--
Is it true that, for every prime $p$, there is a prime $q \leq p$ which is a primitive root modulo $p$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_985 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ᵉ (p : ℕ) (hp_prime : p.Prime) (hp_nontrivial : p ≠ 2),
    ∃ q, q.Prime ∧ q < p ∧ orderOf (q : ZMod p) = p - 1 := by
  sorry

-- TODO: Artin conjectured that 2 is a primitive root for infinitely many primes $p$, which
-- Hooley proved assuming the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis.

/--
Heath-Brown proved that at least one of 2, 3, or 5 is a primitive root for infinitely many primes $p$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_985.variants.two_three_five_primitive_root :
    Set.Infinite
      {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧
      (orderOf (2 : ZMod p) = p - 1 ∨
       orderOf (3 : ZMod p) = p - 1 ∨
       orderOf (5 : ZMod p) = p - 1)} := by
  sorry

end Erdos985

findings.description: The docstring does not match the Lean statement or the source. It reads "for every prime $p$, there is a prime $q \leq p$ which is a primitive root modulo $p$". The Lean statement has `q < p` and adds the hypothesis `p ≠ 2`. (1) `≤` vs `<`: the mathematics is unaffected. q = p is 0 in ZMod p, so it is never a primitive root; I proved in Lean that the `q ≤ p` and `q < p` versions of the statement are equivalent. (2) The docstring does not mention the restriction p ≠ 2. Read literally, the docstring's question has a trivial answer 'no': at p = 2 no prime q ≤ 2 (or q < 2) is a primitive root, and I proved in Lean that the unrestricted claim fails at p = 2. The Lean statement correctly excludes this case, but the docstring neither states nor explains the restriction. AGENTS.md asks that docstring, Lean and source agree, and that a domain restriction excluding a degenerate case be explained.
findings.source_evidence: erdosproblems.com/985 (LaTeX source, and every version in its revision history): "Is it true that, for every prime $p$, there is a prime $q<p$ which is a primitive root modulo $p$?" The site's discussion thread (Woett, 17 Aug 2025): "Of course, $p > 2$ is required." Erdős's original [Er65b] (Some recent advances and current problems in number theory, 1965; scan at users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1965-17.pdf): "it is not even known whether to every p there is a prime q < p which is a primitive root of p."
findings.suggested_fix: Change the docstring to: "Is it true that, for every prime $p > 2$, there is a prime $q < p$ which is a primitive root modulo $p$? (The case $p = 2$ is excluded: there is no prime $q < 2$.)". The Lean statement needs no change.

reformulations.difference: The source says "for every prime p"; the Lean statement quantifies over primes p with `p ≠ 2`.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The literal claim is trivially false at p = 2: there is no prime q < 2 (proved in Lean). The source's discussion thread says "Of course, p > 2 is required", and Erdős's 1965 question is about odd primes. For primes, `p ≠ 2` is the same as `p > 2`. I proved in Lean that the file's statement is equivalent to the version with `2 < p` in place of `p ≠ 2`. So the Lean states exactly the intended open problem. It is not equivalent to the degenerate literal reading, whose answer is trivially 'no'.

reformulations.difference: The Lean states that the set of primes p for which 2, 3 or 5 is a primitive root is infinite. The source states that at least one of 2, 3, 5 is a primitive root for infinitely many primes.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The set is the union S_2 ∪ S_3 ∪ S_5, where S_a = {p prime | orderOf (a : ZMod p) = p - 1}. A finite union is infinite if and only if one of its members is infinite (Set.infinite_union). I proved the ↔ in Lean against `∃ a ∈ {2,3,5}, {p | p.Prime ∧ orderOf (a : ZMod p) = p - 1}.Infinite`.

sources_consulted: https://www.erdosproblems.com/985 (via https://r.jina.ai/ reader; direct access is Cloudflare-blocked)
https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1965-17.pdf (Erdős, Some recent advances and current problems in number theory, 1965; OCR text layer)
https://arxiv.org/e-print/math/0412262 (P. Moree, Artin's primitive root conjecture - a survey)
review.notes:
By the repository's default setting, `answer(sorry)` of type Prop elaborates to `True`, so `#print` shows `True ↔ ∀ p, Nat.Prime p → p ≠ 2 → ∃ q, Nat.Prime q ∧ q < p ∧ orderOf ↑q = p - 1` with q : ℕ. This is expected.

`orderOf (q : ZMod p) = p - 1` is the same encoding of "primitive root" used in Wikipedia/ArtinPrimitiveRootsConjecture.lean. I checked it on concrete values in Lean.

A numerical check with a computable order function found a prime primitive root below p for every odd prime p < 3000; p = 2 is the only failure. This matches OEIS A002233.

Status: the site marks the problem OPEN, and the teorth database says "open". This matches `research open`. The variant is correctly tagged `research solved` (Heath-Brown 1986; confirmed by Moree's survey, which says Heath-Brown's result leaves at most two primes q for which 𝒫(q) is finite, and by Wikipedia's "Corollary 1: at least one of 2, 3, or 5"). I did not read Heath-Brown's paper itself.

Guy's UPINT F9, as quoted in an OEIS A002233 comment, phrases the question as "for any large prime p". The cited source and Erdős's original both say "every p", and the formalization follows them.

The docstring's `q ≤ p` was already present in the original commit (Sep 2025), while the Lean statement has always used `q < p`.
